Note.Name: README
Note.Text:
## Overview

This repository contains the Forsta integration for Research Defender (RD). It
wraps both the client-side scripts that call the RD APIs and the server-side
logic that verifies responses and determines whether a respondent can continue
through the survey.

At a high level the integration:

- Collects RD Search V4 and RD Activity data into two Forsta text-list
  questions, `RD_Search` and `RD_Activity`.
- Validates and hashes RD Search data on the server before trusting the client
  payload.
- Retrieves RD Activity statistics server-side using an API token obtained in
  the browser.
- Aggregates the outcomes into a single-value question
  `research_defender_fail` where `0 = allow respondent to continue`,
  `1 = terminate respondent`.

## Configuration

The implementation is configured in the `consts` script. There are two steps
for configuration the project:

1. Fill in the `projectSettings` object (see comments for instructions)
2. Uncomment one of the template configs depending on the type of project.
   It is vital that this is set selected correctly because all of the termination
   logic depens on the values of this config. The defaults align with the company
   standard settings: 
   https://srcentre.sharepoint.com/:w:/s/AuditRiskandPrivacyCommittee/IQCcJahzDWdjRKFloXNC2qfeASJqFJQ_sPub2XwMWw4XtuQ?e=sUGs8X


## Data flow

1. Landing page (`client/onlineIntro.js`) unhides the intro content and the 
   next button only when RD calls finish. It listens for custom events fired by
   the producer scripts so the respondent cannot continue until responses are
   available.
2. **RD Search (`client/search.js`)** runs client-side, calls the RD Search V4
   endpoint, stores the raw payload and HTTP status into `RD_Search`, then fires
   the completion event.
3. **RD Activity token fetch (`client/activity.js`)** runs client-side, calls the
   RD Activity token endpoint, stores the raw token payload and HTTP status into
   `RD_Activity`, then fires its completion event.
4. **Server script (`rd.js`)** executes after the page submits. It parses and
   validates `RD_Search` via `processSearchResults()`, pulls statistics for
   `RD_Activity` via `processActivityResults()`, and finally computes
   `research_defender_fail` inside `determineOverallPassFail()`.

## Client-side behaviour

### search.js

- Uses `fetch` with credentials and an 8-second timeout supplied by Forsta macros
  (`^getTimeout()^`, `^makeRDSearchURL()^`).
- Writes `status_code` and `raw_response` to `RD_Search`.
- Emits a custom event (`^getSearchEventName()^`) so the intro screen can
  re-enable navigation.

### activity.js

- Calls the RD Activity token endpoint with the public API key. Response text
  goes into `RD_Activity.raw_token_response`, HTTP status into `status_code`.
- Emits a second custom event (`^getActivityEventName()^`) and unhides the intro
  once both events are received.

### onlineIntro.js

- Waits for both events (or detects prefilled hidden inputs) before restoring
  the original intro content and un-hiding buttons, preventing users from
  skipping the RD checks.

## Security considerations

The RD Search V4 endpoint supports signing the request URL with the private key
so Research Defender can confirm it was not tampered with. RD also signs the
response payload: `Validation.Surveys` and `Validation.Respondent` are hashes of
the corresponding entries in the `String` object. Because those string values are
not valid JSON, we extract key-value pairs via regular expressions to ensure the
data we trust matches what was signed. We should pursue a native, structured
response with RD to avoid depending on this workaround.

## HTTP status codes and timeouts

Both client scripts use an 8-second timeout. If a request does not complete in
time, it is aborted; the server interprets this as a failure since allowing the
respondent through would let malicious users block outbound traffic to bypass
screening. Every response captures the HTTP status code so we can differentiate
between network issues and valid RD denials.

What is the aim of the project?

ScreenED is a national research project being led by Researchers at the University of Melbourne in collaboration with other researchers from around Australia. The research aims to develop a screening tool (ScreenED) that assesses the risk of eating disorders in primary school aged children. The tool will be used by parents and health professionals to pick up on a range of eating problems in children soon after they begin.

The ScreenED questions have been developed in collaboration with families as well as researchers and health professionals. All of the questions are safe for families, whether there are eating problems or not.

Who are we looking for?

We are looking for families with a primary school aged child to participate. We welcome all families to participate whether there are concerns about your child's eating or not. It's important for our research to involve all types of families in our project, not just those with eating problems.

We will ask 1 parent and 1 child from the family to participate in the study. To participate, children need to be 5 – 12 years old or receiving primary school education at the time of enrolment.

What will I be asked to do?

This survey is in three parts.
Part A – is for the parent to complete. This checks for eligibility and asks for parental consent to participate for you and your child. (This will take around 5 minutes)
Part B – is for your child to complete. This section asks your child about their eating habits, body image, exercise and physical activity, sleep and how they are feeling. (This will take about 20 minutes to complete)
Part C – is for the parent to complete. This section asks you about your child's eating habits, body image, mental health, strengths or difficulties. (This will take around 15 minutes)

Your answers to the survey questions will help us pick the best questions to use in our final screening tool. Parents may request a copy of their and their child’s answers to the survey and will be reimbursed for their time.

Please download a full copy of the study's Plain Language Statement here.

Child Information Statement

You can download a more detailed copy of this child information sheet here




What is this study about?

 

  • We want to create a set of questions that help adults know when a child is having a hard time with their eating.
  • We are creating one set of questions for children who go to primary school.
  • We are creating another set of questions for parents.
  • We would like you and your parent to be a part of this study.
  • 310 children and their parents are being asked to be a part of this study too.

 


Do I have to be in this study?

 

  • You do not have to do this study if you do not want to.
  • You can talk to your parents about being in the study.
  • You can change your mind. You can say yes and then say no later.

 


What will I do?

This study involves completing a survey with different sets of questions. Part B is completed by you. Parts A and C are completed by your parent.

For your part of the survey (Part B): there are 6 sets of questions. It will take about 20 minutes.

The questions ask about:

  • What you like to eat, how you like to have meals, overeating, and what you might not like about eating
  • how you feel about your body, what kind of exercise you might do, how your sleep was last night and how you feel today.

There are no right or wrong answers. Some of the questions might seem similar to each other. That’s ok. Just give your most true answer each time.

  • Your parent can help you read and understand the questions, but your parent cannot answer the questions for you.
  • If you are not sure what something means, you can ask your parent for help.
  • When you have finished answering your questions, your parent may request a copy of your answers sent to their phone or computer

 


What if I get sad or angry about the questions I am asked?

 

  • Some of the questions could make you feel a bit upset, sad or frustrated. If this happens you can:
    • Talk to your parent about this
    • Talk to a researcher in this study
    • Call Kids Helpline (the phone number is 1800 55 1800) or chat to them online (https://kidshelpline.com.au/kids)
  • You can also stop answering the questions at any time.
  • You do not have to finish the study.

 


What happens after the study?

 

  • We will use your ideas and answers to make the questions better.
  • The questions will be used by parents and children in the future to help kids who are having a hard time with their eating.

FormText.Text: Which eating disorder(s) has your child been diagnosed with?

Texts.Text: Anorexia nervosa is characterised by restriction of energy intake leading to significantly low body weight accompanied by an intense fear of weight gain and body image disturbanceAnorexia Nervosa (AN)

ARFID is characterised by an avoidance or aversion to food and eating that results from heightened sensitivity to sensory aspects of food (such as texture, taste or smell); a lack of interest in food/eating secondary to low appetite, or because of concerns about the harmful effects of food or eating on the body (e.g. worrying about choking or feeling sick). The person may prefer to eat the same food repeatedly, or to seek foods that are predictable, or they may not notice they are hungry and go long periods without eating. Importantly restriction is NOT due to a body image disturbance, but a result of anxiety or phobia of food and/or eating.Avoidant Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID)

Binge eating disorder is characterised by recurrent episodes of binge eating, which involves eating a large amount of food in a short period of time, accompanied by feelings of a loss of control and often linked with high levels of distress. A person with binge eating disorder will not use compensatory behaviours, such as self-induced vomiting or overexercising after binge eating.Binge Eating Disorder (BED)
Bulimia nervosa is characterised by recurrent episodes of binge eating, followed by compensatory behaviours, such as vomiting or excessive exercise to prevent weight gain.Bulimia Nervosa (BN)

A person with OSFED may present with many of the symptoms of other eating disorders such as anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa or binge eating disorder but will not meet the full criteria for diagnosis of these disorders.Other Specified Feeding and Eating Disorders (OSFED)

Unspecified feeding or eating disorder refers to disordered feeding or eating behaviour that causes clinically significant distress, but which does not meet the full criteria for any of the other eating disorder categories. UFED is a category applied to eating disorder presentations in which there is insufficient information to make a more specific diagnosis (e.g., in emergency room settings).Unspecified Feeding or Eating Disorder (UFED)
